title: Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling
authors: Anran Liu, Benzhao Hou, Zongsheng Cao, Daichao Wang, Lang Chen, Shitong Chen
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can turn natural-language optimization tasks into solver-checked answers, but current agents remain brittle under narrative rewrites and often store reusable experience at the instance level. We introduce \textsc{ArchOR}, an archetype-centric skill agent that builds on \textsc{OptSkills} by adding two retrieval-focused modules. \emph{Centroid-Aware Representation Learning} (CARL) refines the ordering of cached skill representations through a low-rank prototype residual. \emph{Signature-Guided Retrieval} (S\textsuperscript{3}R) attaches open-dimensional structural signatures to skills, prioritizes candidates by weighted Jaccard overlap, and bounds semantic re-ranking to a top-$K$ set. A baseline-preserving arbitration rule determines when the structural route should replace the original selector. With the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone and released skill library, \textsc{ArchOR} reaches 65.00\% Micro-Avg.\ Pass@1 across five benchmarks, improving over \textsc{OptSkills} by 1.64~pp Micro-Avg.\ and 2.68~pp Macro-Avg.

infographic.key_insight: ArchOR improves optimization-modeling agents by retrieving reusable skills through structural archetypes rather than relying solely on instance-level similarity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structure-aware retrieval can help engineering optimization agents select relevant modeling skills when problem narratives vary.
method: CARL refines cached skill representation rankings using a low-rank prototype residual.
S³R prioritizes skills by weighted Jaccard overlap of structural signatures, then semantically re-ranks only the top-K candidates.
Baseline-preserving arbitration decides when structural retrieval should replace the original selector.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five benchmarks, ArchOR achieves 65.00% Micro-Avg. Pass@1 with the same DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone and released skill library, outperforming OptSkills by 1.64 percentage points micro-average and 2.68 points macro-average.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify robustness under narrative rewrites or retrieval overhead, leaving deployment trade-offs uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Structure-Aware Skill Retrieval and Arbitration for Optimization Modeling

title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents
authors: Xiangyu Kong, Ruirui Yang, Xia Hou
abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.

infographic.key_insight: Successful negotiation requires executable value, not just agreement: TACTIC improves economic outcomes by adapting to prior settlement results without updating base LLM weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-agent systems should validate negotiated commitments against operational constraints and use execution feedback to refine future strategies.
method: TradeWar converts multi-country negotiations into tariff and trade-share policies, enforcing capacity and network constraints at settlement.
Outcomes are scored using an Economic Health Index (EHI).
TACTIC refines strategies across episodes using prior experience, opponent behavior, and settlement outcomes.

infographic.watch_item: Evaluation is simulation-based and uses three seeds; transfer to real trade negotiations remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
authors: Vipin Kurian Elavunkel, Sylvain Le Tonquesse, Hadrien Vroylandt
abstract: Identifying earth-abundant catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a central challenge in scalable green hydrogen production. We present a computational pipeline that couples diffusion-based generative modelling, machine-learning force-field relaxation, and graph neural network (GNN) property prediction to discover bimetallic HER catalysts beyond the structures and stoichiometries covered by existing adsorption databases. A generative model (MatterGen) is fine-tuned on bulk alloy structures labelled with their minimum hydrogen adsorption energy and steered towards adsorption energies near zero. From the generated pool we retain the stable structures that are novel bimetallic alloys: binary compositions built from the training-set metals but at stoichiometries or structures absent from that database. Each candidate's low-index facets are ranked by a machine-learning-force-field (MatterSim) surface-energy screen, and only the most stable terminations are converted into explicit slab models with hydrogen adsorbed at all high-symmetry surface sites and relaxed with the same force field. Two GNN surrogates (MEGNet and ALIGNN), trained on a high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) dataset, then screen the resulting slab candidates. Because the two models encode the local environment through different inductive biases, we retain only the alloys on which both agree, reducing the influence of any single model. This consensus screening, combined with a MatterSim energy-difference triangulation, resulted in a shortlist of near-thermoneutral bimetallic candidates. Eight are validated with plane-wave DFT, and four of them, Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3, bind hydrogen within the thermoneutral window. All eight alloys are dynamically stable by phonon calculations. These four alloys are highlighted as DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates for experimental follow-up.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-driven design pipeline identified four novel bimetallic HER catalyst candidates with DFT-validated near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding: Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining generative design with surrogate screening can prioritize alloy compositions and surface structures for costly DFT evaluation and experimental follow-up.
method: Fine-tune MatterGen on adsorption-labelled bulk alloys to generate novel binaries targeting near-zero hydrogen adsorption energy.
Use MatterSim to screen surface stability and relax hydrogen-adsorbed slabs at high-symmetry sites.
Shortlist candidates using MEGNet–ALIGNN consensus and MatterSim energy differences, then validate with DFT and phonon calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of eight alloys evaluated with plane-wave DFT, four met the thermoneutral hydrogen-binding criterion; all eight were dynamically stable by phonon calculations.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental HER activity and durability remain unverified, and the four highlighted candidates contain precious metals despite the earth-abundance motivation.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction

title: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective
authors: Yuxin Chen, Yuejie Chi, Jianqing Fan, Gen Li, Yuting Wei, Yuling Yan
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) embodies a foundational paradigm for sequential decision-making in the face of uncertainty. The rapid growth of model complexity in emerging applications has significantly amplified the challenges of achieving data-efficient RL, particularly in sample-starved scenarios where data collection may be costly, time-consuming, or even high-stakes. Consequently, understanding and improving the data efficiency of RL algorithms has become a central problem of both fundamental theoretical interest and practical importance. Despite decades of research, the statistical underpinnings of RL remained remarkably underdeveloped until relatively recently, particularly in the finite-sample regimes most relevant to modern practice. Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

infographic.key_insight: This monograph explains finite-sample foundations of data-efficient reinforcement learning, emphasizing minimax-optimal algorithms for tabular Markov decision processes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its sample-complexity perspective can guide algorithm selection when interaction data are costly, limited, or high-stakes.
method: Analyze generative-model, online, and offline sampling settings.
Cover model-based and model-free approaches through non-asymptotic sample complexity.
Emphasize statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs and sharp guarantees for widely used algorithms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes theoretical analyses and statistical guarantees, but reports no empirical datasets, benchmarks, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The primary treatment assumes tabular MDPs, so guarantees should not be assumed to transfer directly to deep RL or large continuous spaces.
infographic.paper_title: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective

title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
authors: Anastasiia Prutianova, Alina Bogdanova, Mikhail Shutov, Dmitrii Poimanov, Anatoly Gorkov, Ilia Zharikov
abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: TVQ makes vector-quantized LLM weights trainable, enabling gradient-based recovery of quality lost under extreme compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: TVQ offers a practical route to low-bit LLM deployment with a modest training budget and a straightforward PyTorch implementation.
method: Use trainable latent weights and straight-through estimation to optimize discrete vector-quantized weights.
Apply block-wise knowledge distillation to balance model quality and training efficiency.
Support objectives beyond layer-wise reconstruction loss and integration with modern VQ schemes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-lossless 2-bit quantization of LLaMA2-70B, with only a 1% accuracy drop on popular question-answering benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify training costs or measured inference speedups, so deployment efficiency requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models

title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling
authors: Vsevolod Biryukov, Sergey V. Barabash, Pranab Kumar Das, Jack Deslippe, Mauro Del Ben, Felipe H. da Jornada
abstract: Quantum-mechanical approaches, such as density functional theory (DFT), underpin much of modern computational materials science and are the primary source of data for AI-driven discovery. Yet the established electronic-structure codes today represent decades-old software architectures, making new physical models slow and costly to implement, validate, and deploy on emerging hardware. We present Quantum 3xplorer (Q3, pronounced "Quantum Explorer"), an AI-native quantum simulation engine written from scratch by AI coding agents under the direction and supervision of domain scientists. As a first and demanding validation case, we implement plane-wave pseudopotential DFT end to end: norm-conserving, ultrasoft, and projector-augmented-wave formalisms, spin polarization, DFT+U, and dispersion corrections, together with forces, stresses, structural relaxation, and electronic-structure analysis. Q3 reproduces established reference implementations, runs faster on a single core in representative benchmarks, and scales across GPU-accelerated supercomputers. It was developed in weeks rather than years. Its layered, physics-first architecture separates abstract quantum-mechanical concepts from their numerical representations, making its framework extendable beyond plane waves to other basis sets and levels of theory. Its inputs and outputs follow structured, schema-validated data standards, making every result AI-ready. Q3 is open source under Apache 2.0 and built to be reused, extended, and improved by the research community. Q3 points to a paradigm shift in how computational quantum science is done. Scientists define the physics, formulate the models, and set the criteria for validation; AI agents write, test, and optimize the code. The decades-long path from a new theory to a trusted, high-performance implementation can thus collapse to days, significantly accelerating scientific discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum 3xplorer (Q3) demonstrates scientist-supervised, AI-agent development of a quantum simulation engine in weeks rather than years.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its layered architecture and schema-validated inputs and outputs aim to simplify physics extensions, hardware adaptation, and integration into AI-driven materials workflows.
method: Domain scientists define physics and validation criteria; AI agents write, test, and optimize code.
Implement end-to-end plane-wave pseudopotential DFT with multiple formalisms, forces, stresses, and structural relaxation.

infographic.paper_title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling

title: Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zhuguanyu Wu, Congjia Chen, Ruihao Gong, Yang Yong, Shiqiao Gu, Yi Xu
abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl

infographic.key_insight: Geo-FSRL selects stochastic transitions that minimize update-induced conditional KL divergence within a coefficient-preserving Gaussian policy family for few-step flow reinforcement learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It improves reinforcement-learning fine-tuning on the original few-step schedule while retaining the deterministic solver at inference.
method: Reduce policy selection to a scalar geometry factor governing conditional KL, velocity-space Fisher information, and log-likelihood-ratio variance.
Derive a unique closed-form optimum using both source and target noise levels, shared across all nonzero velocity updates.
Apply gradient-scale matching with closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights to normalize timestep-dependent scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image and video generation models in the 4-step setting, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: The optimality guarantee is restricted to the specified coefficient-preserving isotropic Gaussian family; broader policy families and step counts require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Optimizing Stochastic Policy Geometry for Few-Step Flow Reinforcement Learning

title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service
authors: Saiful Khan, Yiwen Xing, Joyraj Chakraborty, Afrah Farea, Philip Beaucamp, Samuel Jackson
abstract: In modern data infrastructure, a data virtualization service (DVS) allows users to create many versions of source datasets for different processing tasks. For example, a multivariate or multi-modality dataset can be used for different machine learning tasks (e.g., classification, detection, segmentation, forecasting, and so on). Data selection, participation, integration, and preprocessing in different tasks result in many virtual datasets [Khan et al., SSC 2026]. Meanwhile, different users need to discover existing virtual datasets frequently and easily to avoid duplicate efforts. To enable an effective search engine in a DVS, it is desirable to automatically generate keywords for each virtual dataset. In this work, we present a solution for generating keywords for virtual datasets using large language models (LLMs). We propose five strategies for selecting different collections of text data for processing by the LLMs. We applied the five strategies to virtual datasets created in five application case studies with different source datasets. We conducted experiments with three LLM generators and two embedding techniques. The experiments show that the performances of the five strategies depend on the quality of the text descriptions. The results help us adopt a multi-strategy implementation of a new keyword generation service (KGS) as part of an extended DVS. The work demonstrates that the capability of automated keyword generation is indispensable for a high-volume DVS that is dataset-rich and frequently accessed.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated keywords can support virtual dataset discovery, but text-description quality affects which generation strategy performs best.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A multi-strategy keyword generation service can help users find existing virtual datasets and avoid duplicating data preparation work.
method: Define five strategies for selecting text to feed into LLM keyword generators.
Evaluate three LLM generators and two embedding techniques.
Adopt a multi-strategy keyword generation service within an extended data virtualization service.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments covered virtual datasets from five application case studies with different source datasets, showing that strategy performance depends on text-description quality.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative performance or scaling results, leaving deployment accuracy, latency, and cost uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Keyword Generation Using LLMs in a High-Volume Data Virtualization Service

title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
authors: Nicolò Pagan, Michael Andreas Ebling, Stefania Ionescu, Anikó Hannák
abstract: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.

infographic.key_insight: AI hiring evaluators favor applications written by certain models, independently of candidate qualifications, and also favor their own outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: AI screening systems should be audited for writer-model and stylistic biases that can penalize qualified applicants based on their choice of writing tool.
method: Pair 11 LLM writers with 9 API-hosted evaluators across 10 job descriptions and 50 candidates per job.
Compare evaluator acceptance across writer models to identify preference hierarchies and self-preference.
Analyze stylistic cues to explain preferences and test for residual writer fingerprints.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the most adverse writer–evaluator pairing, approximately 1.8 of 25 qualified candidates were filtered out purely because of model mismatch.
infographic.watch_item: The audit covers a specific model and job-description set; screening systems need renewed testing as models and deployment conditions change.
infographic.paper_title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality

title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments
authors: Philipp Bordne, André Biedenkapp
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful framework for sequential decision-making. Despite many high-profile successes in recent years, deep RL is known to be brittle. An emerging line of research attributes this brittleness to a loss of plasticity in neural networks. However, plasticity loss has so far been understudied in stochastic environments. We study this interplay systematically, training SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks augmented with controlled levels of observation and action noise. We find that plasticity-preserving methods increase learning robustness on the two harder tasks, with their advantage growing as observation noise increases, while combining resets with layer normalization underperforms resets alone at every observation noise level tested. Further, stochasticity can accelerate the loss of plasticity in harder environments, whereas in easier settings noise can act as a regularizer that sustains plasticity. Lastly, plasticity loss is most pronounced in the early stages of training. In the most challenging stochastic settings, TD instability rather than gradual plasticity loss becomes the dominant failure mode.

infographic.key_insight: Plasticity-preserving methods improve deep RL robustness on harder tasks as observation noise increases, but extreme stochasticity shifts the main failure mode to TD instability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For noisy control systems, evaluate plasticity interventions alongside TD stability rather than assuming that preserving plasticity alone ensures reliable learning.
method: Train SAC agents on three DeepMind Control tasks.
Vary controlled levels of observation and action noise.
Compare plasticity-preserving methods, including resets and resets combined with layer normalization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the three tasks, robustness gains appeared on the two harder tasks and grew with observation noise; resets combined with layer normalization underperformed resets alone at every observation-noise level tested.
infographic.watch_item: Effects depend on task difficulty: noise can sustain plasticity in easier settings, so intervention benefits should not be assumed to generalize beyond the tested tasks.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Understanding the Impact of Plasticity Loss on Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Environments

title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
authors: Shengguang Wu, Suning Huang, Cherie Ho, Ria Doshi, Hao Zhu, Serena Yeung-Levy
abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.

infographic.key_insight: RoboArchitect automatically improves robotic manipulation by evolving the control harness and persistent memory around a frozen policy, without updating model weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated harness design offers an alternative to policy finetuning when adapting robots to new tasks or environments.
method: A coding model observes robot rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises control code.
The harness coordinates policy queries, vision tools, and direct arm commands.
Persistent memory carries learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple benchmarks and policies, average success rose from 9.7% to 43.3% on held-out scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on held-out tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify optimization cost or safety requirements for executing automatically generated robot-control code.
infographic.paper_title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory

title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
authors: Abdul Fatir Ansari, Oleksandr Shchur, Jaris Küken, Andreas Auer, Boran Han, Pedro Mercado
abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.

infographic.key_insight: Chronos-2 delivers zero-shot probabilistic forecasts by learning interactions among multiple time series and heterogeneous covariates without task-specific training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single pretrained model could reduce domain-specific forecasting development while providing uncertainty estimates and fast inference for scientific and engineering systems.
method: Uses large-scale pretraining for cross-domain forecasting.
Infers relationships among time series and covariates from historical context.
Generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports average skill-score gains of 5.2 percentage points over the strongest baselines, a 10-percentage-point increase in win rates, and forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU.
infographic.watch_item: Validate accuracy and uncertainty calibration on the target system; average benchmark gains do not guarantee reliable performance in every domain.
infographic.paper_title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting

title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
authors: Sloan Nietert, Daniel Kuhn
abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $κ$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.

infographic.key_insight: For Wasserstein-robust linear regression, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR) achieve minimax regret rates, while standard DRO can be suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: When regression models face distribution shift, optimizing worst-case excess risk rather than worst-case risk can improve robustness relative to the best predictor for each target distribution.
method: Model source-to-target shift as an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of radius ε.
Characterize small-shift regret through a problem-specific condition number κ.
Develop an exact convex reformulation for MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical minimax-rate results, high-probability finite-sample guarantees, and numerical experiments separating MRO and SNR performance from DRO.
infographic.watch_item: The results concern multivariate least-squares regression under Wasserstein-bounded shifts; the abstract does not establish applicability to other losses or shift models.
infographic.paper_title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression

title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger
authors: Akshay Balsubramani
abstract: Instance-dependent limits for bandit regret, sequential tests, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes are proved by one chain. It runs from a divergence decomposition through data processing to a statistic, a testing step that turns a class guarantee into a requirement on the history, and optimization over alternatives and allocations. Only the first step is an identity. This work writes the chain as an exact ledger. By the chain rule, data processing loses exactly a conditional divergence, which vanishes for arms in natural exponential families at the per-arm counts and reward sums. A one-parameter family of martingale identities extends the decomposition to every tilt between two instances. The classical limits follow by relaxations with named defects. All defects but the asymptotic step's can be computed from an algorithm's own runs, the uniform quantification's only when the class guarantee is a number. On seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger locates the difference between standard algorithms and the classical limits. For identification among trained models and for Wald's test the largest term is usually the uniform quantification's.

infographic.key_insight: Classical instance-dependent limits can be expressed as an exact information ledger that names the losses introduced after the initial divergence identity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The ledger helps diagnose gaps between sequential algorithms and classical limits in bandits, hypothesis testing, best-arm identification and Markov decision processes.
method: Track divergence through data processing, testing and optimization over alternatives and allocations.
Express data-processing loss as conditional divergence; it vanishes at per-arm counts and reward sums for natural exponential families.
Extend the decomposition across instance tilts using a one-parameter family of martingale identities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven published sources, from movie ratings to engine replacement, the ledger attributes algorithm–limit gaps; uniform quantification is usually the largest term for trained-model identification and Wald’s test.
infographic.watch_item: The asymptotic defect is not computable from an algorithm’s own runs, and the uniform-quantification defect requires a numerical class guarantee.
infographic.paper_title: Instance-dependent sequential limits as an exact information ledger

title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT
authors: Vitaly Feldman, Moshe Shenfeld
abstract: In the random allocation sampling scheme each user's data is used in $k$ steps chosen randomly and uniformly from a sequence of $t$ steps. This scheme is known to improve on Poisson sampling in private optimization and in communication-efficient aggregation. The existing privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant for this scheme runs in time quadratic in the inverse of the accuracy parameter $α$ (Feldman and Shenfeld, 2026). We give an algorithm, \emph{multiscale FFT}, that represents likelihood ratios on a grid that is uniform within each dyadic interval and computes the exact rounding of every pairwise sum using FFTs within each interval. It keeps the guarantees of the accountant and improves the dependence of its running time on $α$ from $O(α^{-2})$ to $O(α^{-1}\log(1/α))$. In addition, we demonstrate that rounding can be performed via the mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection of (Doroshenko et al., 2026). This reduces the errors that rounding introduces in the mean of the privacy loss and in the $χ^2$ divergence of the computed pair from the order of $α$ to $O(α^2/\log(t))$. In our experiments, our algorithm achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and gives improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.

infographic.key_insight: Multiscale FFT accelerates random-allocation privacy accounting, improving accuracy-dependent runtime from O(α⁻²) to O(α⁻¹ log(1/α)) while preserving the accountant’s guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster high-accuracy privacy accounting can make random-allocation DP-SGD and communication-efficient aggregation more practical.
method: Represent likelihood ratios on grids that are uniform within each dyadic interval.
Use interval-wise FFTs to compute the exact rounding of every pairwise sum.
Apply mean-preserving connect-the-dots projection to reduce rounding errors in mean privacy loss and χ² divergence to O(α²/log(t)).
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report speedups of several orders of magnitude at high accuracy and improved privacy bounds for DP-SGD with PREAMBLE.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify benchmark sizes or hardware, so practical speedups require validation on the intended workload.
infographic.paper_title: Fast Privacy Loss Accounting for Random Allocation via Multiscale FFT

title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
authors: Yuzhe Liu, Haolin Tian, Tonghan Wang
abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.

infographic.key_insight: ACCT lets different-sized LLMs within the same model family reuse context computation by converting a source model’s KV cache into sparse KV states for a target model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Heterogeneous LLM deployments could reduce repeated context-processing costs when switching models without requiring the target to prefill the original context.
method: Cartographer selects query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head.
Allocator distributes a shared KV token budget across target layers and heads.
Compiler transforms selected source KV entries into target-compatible sparse KV states.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five general-capability benchmarks and six context-dependent tasks, ACCT matched or exceeded target-model performance with 75% smaller KV caches; at approximately 19K context tokens, KV conversion was 6.5–21.2× faster than target context prefill.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover different-sized models within the same family; compatibility across model families and end-to-end deployment gains remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer

title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tomás Figliolia, Beren Millidge
abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

infographic.key_insight: Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA) uses a tree-structured indexer to make sparse attention asymptotically subquadratic, including routing costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ZHA offers a path to longer-context pretrained LLMs through lightweight adaptation rather than training from scratch.
method: Recursively compress cached keys into a hierarchy of summaries.
Route queries top-down to select a sparse subset of keys for attention.
Increase tree depth with sequence length to keep per-query routing and attention costs sublinear.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports adaptation via KL distillation over a few billion tokens, preserved retrieval and reasoning performance, robustness with trees up to six levels, and modeled scaling advantages beyond one million tokens.
infographic.watch_item: Hundreds-of-millions-to-billions-token contexts remain a projected capability; practical gains depend on efficient routing, memory management, and hardware implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer

title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Iulia Rusu, Anoop Praturu, Sergei Gepshtein, Tatyana Sharpee
abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) seeks to infer the reward function underlying observed behavior, but its predictive accuracy and interpretability depend on how that reward is computed from the underlying features. While prior IRL reward functions have been implemented through a variety of techniques including linear weights, neural networks, or other function approximators, none make assumptions about the geometry of the underlying feature space. Inspired by geometric organization observed in neural circuits, we introduce Hyperbolic inverse reinforcement learning (Hyperbolic IRL), which parameterizes reward as a function of Hyperbolic distance between the feature vector and a learned parameter vector, as well as its Euclidean distance variant. We tested our methods against a range of linear and nonlinear IRL baselines under both deterministic and stochastic policies. Our Hyperbolic approach achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on established benchmarks and excelled in the low data limit and across dense environments. Applied to human navigation among multiple exhibits in a museum room, Hyperbolic IRL reveals reward structure that depends not only on individual exhibit-distance features, but also on non-separable conjunctions between them. Together, these results demonstrate that a Hyperbolic reward parameterization can improve both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of IRL, providing a framework for studying how non-separable, conjunctive structure can begin to explain behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Hyperbolic IRL models rewards using hyperbolic distance, capturing non-separable feature interactions while improving prediction in low-data and dense environments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Geometry-aware reward models offer a way to infer behavior from limited demonstrations while exposing interactions that linear reward models cannot represent.
method: Parameterize reward using hyperbolic distance between a feature vector and a learned parameter vector.
Evaluate a Euclidean-distance variant alongside linear and nonlinear IRL baselines.
Analyze human museum navigation to reveal joint effects of exhibit-distance features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across established benchmarks with deterministic and stochastic policies, Hyperbolic IRL matched state-of-the-art performance overall and excelled with limited data and in dense environments.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify gains or computational costs, leaving practical trade-offs and generalization beyond the tested settings uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Hyperbolic Inverse Reinforcement Learning

title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
authors: Long Vu, Jongseong Brad Choi, Binoy Ravindran, Zhoulai Fu
abstract: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.

infographic.key_insight: Stopping freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization when no candidate’s expected improvement exceeds its incremental cost is simple and cost-aware, but can stop prematurely at low costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The rule provides a cost-aware reference for resumable hyperparameter tuning, trading model scores against training increments without requiring a fixed budget.
method: Maximize best observed score minus cost per training increment.
Under a fixed surrogate, advance the candidate with highest expected improvement; stop when none exceeds cost.
Use a lower bound on two-step lookahead value to certify premature stops; repeated corrections do not lower expected utility under the surrogate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test found EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gained at low costs on two benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Expected-utility guarantees depend on the surrogate; stronger information sharing improved EI stopping’s utility, highlighting sensitivity to surrogate design.
infographic.paper_title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?

title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
authors: Artin Yousefi, Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Lorien C Abroms, David A Broniatowski
abstract: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.

infographic.key_insight: Across six LLMs, smoking-cessation advice varied by user persona; a factual-floor system prompt reduced these differences but did not consistently improve overall fact coverage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Health-advice systems need model-specific validation of age-aware factual safeguards while allowing tone and vocabulary to adapt to users.
method: Asked six LLMs from four providers the same four cessation questions using 12 personas.
Audited factual coverage across personas differing in life stage, expertise, and smoking history.
Tested a short system prompt specifying core medical facts to include when relevant.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2,880 responses, every model mentioned FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often for teen than adult personas, by 32–67 percentage points; five of six provided fewer facts to a healthcare-expert persona than to one presenting no expertise.
infographic.watch_item: Persona differences do not isolate individual attributes, and equal medication mention rates are not necessarily clinically appropriate because prescription cessation pharmacotherapy is not recommended for minors.
infographic.paper_title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
